A license is a contract. When you agree to a EULA, even though it has the word license in it, you are agreeing to a contract, and are thereby contractually obliged to follow the articles/clauses outlined in that license. This isn't what some lawyer's interpretation, that is the definition. Rather than state a license, which isn't ubiquitously applicable, the word contract is used. If you and I shake hands and make a deal, that's a verbal contract. If it so happens that it's in a professional capacity, it just became a commercial contract as well. Say for example, I am a software developer, offer you some proprietary code, I may not necessarily 'license' it as such, but I can make you sign a contract outlining fair use and expectations etc. After you've read enough legal documents, you will begin to notice differences in languages and word choices. If you notice anywhere there is something to do with end user or consumer rights, there are words like obliged and reasonable expectation. When something needs to be iron clad, like in this instance, they use the lowest common denominator, in this case, a contract as well as encompassing language, like 'Nothing' as is the case in the article. Lesson from that, a license is a contract.

The "Party"s are the national governments that sign the treaty. It's saying that governments can't force foreign software creators to hand over their source code. But some commenters here have misunderstood it.

If you write source code "MMM" that compiles to mmm.exe, and you GPL this code, right now, Oracle (or whomever) is free to take MMM and add to it (MMM-Oracle), but if they want to SELL their new mmm-oracle.exe, anyone they sell it to (or give it to) can request the source code (MMM-Oracle). This means that if the maintainers of MMM (in this example, you) like the stuff in there, you can incorporate it into your baseline and distribute it to anyone for free (or for a million dollars, but you'll be handing over your source code in each case).

Now, if Oracle instead made MMM-Oracle, and compiled it to mmm-oracle.exe, and sold that, and then REFUSED to hand out the resultant source code, the GOVERNMENT (the "party") has to enforce that. They have to make Oracle obey the GPL.

No Party shall require the transfer of, or access to, source code of software owned by a person of another Party, as a condition for the import, distribution, sale or use of such software, or of products containing such software, in its territory.

What is meant by "Party" here is: a state that is a party to this treaty. In other words, any signatory country.

A "person of another Party," is a citizen or corporation from a foreign country which is also a signatory to the treaty.

"[S]oftware owned by a person of another Party," is software whose copyright holder is a citizen or corporation from a foreign country which is also a signatory to the treaty.

This DOES NOT AFFECT THE GPL (or any other software license).

Also, this language does not prohibit requirement of source code of software for the purpose of CERTIFICATION. (like: security certification). If you don't have the time that means you're going too fast. Depending on the parachute, you'll need to be under 10,000m and going less than 200m/s. One great way to do this that requires almost no fuel is as you close in on Kerbin (I'm assuming your coming back home when having this issue) set your periapsis to around 45,000 to 50,000m or so, then use your RCS to keep the flattest part of your craft facing the direction you're traveling. You'll need to make a few passes but after a few rounds, your Apoapsis will get closer and closer to Kerbin. Then a couple more passes and you'll have a very smooth arch that will cut you through the lower atmosphere. Once you have that trajectory, try to go in heat shield first and create more drag (if you have an engine and fuel still, you can slow yourself down faster by kicking retro), and then as you fall more you should slow down enough to open your chutes. They may not open completely until you're closer to the ground but they'll open, so don't worry.

tl;dr: My guess is you're just heading in too straight and too fast. More laps through the upper atmosphere to slow yourself down.
Post a picture of your map view that shows your trajectory before reentry.

Re entry is tricky in the latter versions. You have to have a near circular orbit with a pe just inside the atmosphere to bring it down slow. Don't deploy your parachutes until your speed is under 300 m/s
Set your periapsis to about 30k m and use aerobraking to scrub v. You will get down to about 250m/s at 4k M altitude. Ride it out until you're at about 1500m then pop your chutes.

A couple things. The aerobraking thing is a great idea, plus it saves fuel. Most of the time your ship won't get hot if you have fuel tanks and a few engines on, if you keep it aligned inline with the trajectory. But it's probably still safe to decouple these to expose a heat shield.

Don't head straight into Earth perpendicularly. Take a long trip in the atmosphere, alter the trajectory just barely enough to get rid of the periapsis, but little more. Land in the ocean if you can, eyeballing mountains can be tricky (for me at least), and if you reenter at night...try your damnedest to land in the ocean. Because you won't be seeing shit and might crash.
